Package org.aeonbits.owner.formats.json

Class JsonLoader

java.lang.Object
org.aeonbits.owner.formats.json.JsonLoader
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable, Loader
public class JsonLoader extends Object implements Loader
A loader for JSON, reading a source whose path ends in .json. 
     {
       "server": { "host": "localhost", "port": 8080 },
       "servers": [ { "host": "alpha" }, { "host": "beta" } ]
     }
 
     server.host=localhost
     server.port=8080
     servers[0].host=alpha
     servers[1].host=beta

The keys are the ones every loader in this library flattens to, so what a JSON document produces is read by the same nested interfaces, indexed lists and grouped maps as anything else. Nothing here is specific to JSON except the parsing.

A value is kept as it was written. A number is not read into a double and printed back — 1e3 stays 1e3 — because every value in this library is text until a converter is asked for a type, and the conversion is the caller's to declare.

A null writes nothing at all, and the key is simply not there. A Properties cannot hold a null, so this is the only faithful reading available: the alternative, an empty value, would give "" two meanings and is the choice Spring has been unable to move away from for a decade. Typesafe Config arrives at the same place from the other side — a null exists in its object model and the reading API treats it as missing.

The cost has to be stated because it cannot be seen: no method signature in this library can tell absent from explicitly null, both being null or an empty Optional. So a @DefaultValue wins over a null written on purpose, which is not what the author of {"proxy": null} meant. Write the key out of the document when that matters, or give the method no default.

An empty array is an empty value, servers=, which the library already reads as an empty collection — a faithful reading, and one that overrides a default, as the document says. An empty object writes nothing: a section with nothing in it has nothing to say.

A repeated name is refused. RFC 8259 leaves that case undefined and most parsers keep the last value, which is reading half of an ambiguous document instead of saying it is ambiguous. JSON has a real way to write a list, so a repeated name is a mistake rather than a shorthand — which is why the answer differs from the one INI and XML give to a repeated key, where the repetition is the list.

    • defaultSpecFor

      public String defaultSpecFor(String urlPrefix)
      Description copied from interface: Loader
      Returns the default URI specification for a given URI resource, that can be handled by this loader.

      Returning null means this loader adds nothing to the sources looked for in the absence of @Sources - which is what SystemLoader and DotEnvLoader both do, since neither is named after the configuration interface. That is also why this method has a default: it is a choice a loader is allowed to decline, and declining it should not require writing a method that returns nothing.

      A loader offering more than one name - a format spelled .yaml and .yml, or .ini and .cfg - overrides Loader.defaultSpecsFor(String) instead. The two are not meant to be overridden together.

      Specified by:
      defaultSpecFor in interface Loader
      Parameters:
      urlPrefix - the prefix identifying the URI resource.
      Returns:
      the default URI specification for a given URI resource, or null for none.
